lines.text: Your fridge doesn't make anything cold. It does something far stranger: it moves heat.
Inside its pipes runs a liquid that boils far below freezing. Follow it around the loop.
Step one, the evaporator, inside the fridge. The liquid boils here, soaking up heat from your food. That's the cold.
Step two, the compressor. It squeezes the vapor, and squeezing makes it hot, far hotter than your kitchen.
Step three, the condenser, the coils on the back. The vapor is hotter than the room, so heat flows out, and it turns back into liquid.
Step four, the expansion valve. A tiny opening drops the pressure, the liquid flashes cold, and the loop begins again.
The secret is pressure. Low pressure, and it boils at a freezing temperature. High pressure, and it condenses while hot.
So where does the heat go? Into your kitchen. Leave the door open, and the room only gets warmer.
Three tips. Clean the coils twice a year. Test the door seal with a dollar bill. Keep it near forty degrees Fahrenheit.
Watch again, and follow one molecule around the loop.
